text: Fourteen deliverables and a strategy document still aren't a presentation. This lesson compresses all of it into a story Dana Whitfield can deliver in minutes.

Boards listen for four things: time compressed to seconds, not slides; risk stated in dollars, not compliance jargon; a roadmap that reads as momentum, not a wishlist; and one specific ask instead of vague support.

The hook opens exactly where Lesson 1 did: a six-week DSAR, two conflicting order histories, a problem that already reached the board. The cost of inaction follows immediately — staff hours already spent, framed against UK GDPR's real penalty ceiling.

What we built isn't fourteen lesson titles — it's four outcomes: named owners, one reconciled golden record, governed AI pilots instead of unmonitored ones, and a real architecture for Summit. The roadmap presents four phases as proven momentum, not a plan still on paper.

The ask is three specific things: fund the Lesson 14 architecture into production, staff Marcus Ibe's governance office for its permanent operational work, and renew Dana Whitfield's mandate for the next phase.

The same incident opens every version of this presentation because the room already half-remembers it — it reached the board once already. That makes the ask land as finishing something known, not funding something new.
Next: Lesson 18 closes out the LTV Global story and looks back on everything this capstone built.
